questions.stem: Avg cost of cross-border transfer per the passage:
questions.passage_context:
Cross-border payments have been one of the most stubborn frictions in global finance — slow, expensive, opaque, and often dependent on correspondent banking relationships that introduce intermediation costs. Even in 2025, sending money across borders typically takes 1-3 business days and costs an average of 6.4% of the transferred amount, according to World Bank data. This is far higher than the UN's Sustainable Development Goal target of 3% by 2030.

India has emerged as a leader in attempting to reduce these frictions. The 2023 launch of cross-border UPI linkages with Singapore (PayNow integration), followed by similar linkages with UAE, France, Mauritius, Sri Lanka, and Bhutan, has pioneered a new model: instant, low-cost, retail-grade cross-border transfers. Under these arrangements, an Indian customer can transfer up to a daily limit (currently ₹1 lakh per transaction in many corridors) using a UPI ID, with funds reaching the foreign recipient within seconds.

The architecture relies on bilateral agreements between NPCI International (NIPL — the international arm of NPCI) and foreign payment systems. These agreements specify foreign-exchange rate methodologies, anti-money-laundering protocols, and dispute-resolution mechanisms. Importantly, settlement happens between the two payment systems at scheduled times, while end-customer experience is instant.

Yet expansion has been gradual. Each new corridor requires extensive coordination with central banks, compliance with diverse AML/KYC frameworks, and currency-conversion arrangements. Wider rollout to G20 economies — particularly the US and EU — faces additional complexity given dollar dominance and the role of SWIFT and traditional correspondent banking. RBI is also exploring CBDC-based cross-border payments, which could fundamentally reduce settlement risk and intermediation costs.

The strategic implications are significant. India sends and receives over USD 100 billion in remittances annually — the world's largest recipient. Reducing remittance costs by even 1 percentage point would save Indian families USD 1 billion annually. Cross-border UPI is not just a technological achievement; it is a diplomatic and economic instrument that could reshape India's international financial influence.
questions.explanation: Para 1: 'costs an average of 6.4% of the transferred amount'.
